narrative.text: A blank page with no extracted text.
A blank page with no extracted text.
The Chinese title page of the UNFPA/WHO guidance on preparing for the introduction of HPV vaccines for national policy and programmes.
The Chinese copyright and disclaimer page of the 2006 HPV vaccine guidance, with WHO Press ordering and permissions details; the extracted text is fragmented.

The Chinese table of contents of the HPV vaccine guidance, listing sections from cervical cancer and HPV through target populations, advocacy, service delivery, monitoring, stewardship and financing; the extracted text splits headings from page numbers.

The Chinese acknowledgements page, explaining that the guidance is based on a March 2006 UNFPA/WHO technical consultation in Montreux and listing participating experts and staff and the WHO departments involved. The extracted text is fragmented, with names and lines cut off.

The Chinese introduction to the HPV vaccine guidance, explaining its purpose of alerting reproductive health, immunization and cancer programmes to key issues. It describes cervical cancer burden (about 500,000 cases and 250,000 deaths a year, mostly in low-income countries), its link to HPV types 16 and 18, the natural history of infection and screening options such as VIA with cryotherapy. The extracted text interleaves columns and is hard to follow.

A Chinese page describing the 2005 World Health Assembly resolution on cancer prevention and control, which urged attention to preventable cancers and research on a cervical cancer vaccine, with a figure on HPV infection, pre-cancer and cancer by age; the text appears twice in the extraction.

Describes in Chinese the two prophylactic HPV vaccines based on virus-like particles, both targeting HPV 16 and 18 and one also types 6 and 11, with near 100% protection against related cervical pre-cancer in trials. A figure shows HPV type distribution in cervical cancer by region; the extracted text is fragmented.

Continues in Chinese on vaccine efficacy against genital warts and regional variation, ongoing research on duration of protection and special groups, and the ideal target population of girls before sexual debut, with licensing expected for ages 9–26. A footnote notes the expected registration of Gardasil and Cervarix in 2006–2007; the text is fragmented.

Discusses in Chinese other groups that might benefit from HPV vaccination, including males, children under 9, people living with HIV, pregnant women and older women, noting that evidence for each is still lacking. The extracted text is fragmented.

Describes in Chinese the innovative features of HPV vaccines, linking them to the 2004 global reproductive health strategy and noting the novelty for sexual and reproductive health of a vaccine against a sexually transmitted cancer cause. It mentions the challenge of extending immunization beyond infants; parts of the text are duplicated and interleaved.

Outlines in Chinese the Global Immunization Vision and Strategy goals to 2015 and how HPV vaccines fit its expanded scope beyond infants, along with roles for cancer control and HIV programmes. The extracted text mixes columns.

Discusses in Chinese the HPV vaccine as an opportunity for STI prevention education and as an expensive product, noting likely high prices for developing countries, possible GAVI support and the risk of private-sector introduction widening inequities. It also covers cultural sensitivities in vaccinating young girls; the text is fragmented.

A short Chinese passage on synergies between immunization, cancer control and reproductive health programmes and the need for international partnerships to secure affordable prices and supply for developing countries; the text is fragmentary.

Covers in Chinese advocacy, information and communication for HPV vaccines, stressing balanced public education about HPV, cervical cancer and the vaccines' benefits and limits. It lists key messages, such as HPV causing 99% of cervical cancers, its high transmissibility, and that vaccines protect only against certain types and not other STIs including HIV.

Continues in Chinese the key messages, noting that about 30% of cervical cancers are not prevented by current vaccines so screening must continue, and advising culturally sensitive messaging that includes boys. It begins the advocacy action points; the text is fragmented.

Describes in Chinese tailored messages for policy-makers, programme managers and providers and for civil society and professional groups, covering disease burden, programme benefits, screening methods, partnerships and vaccine safety. The extracted text is fragmented.

Discusses in Chinese HPV vaccine service delivery to the primary target group of young adolescent girls through school-based or immunization programme approaches, drawing on reproductive health programmes' experience with sensitive topics. The text is fragmented.

Describes in Chinese the secondary target group of unvaccinated women aged 14–26, whose coverage depends on national resources, and the need to keep screening older and vaccinated women. It advises against stand-alone HPV programmes and urges using existing systems such as the vaccine cold chain.

Discusses in Chinese partnerships between national immunization, reproductive health, adolescent health, cancer and HIV programmes, education and civil society, and monitoring and evaluation, including adverse event reporting with HIV and pregnancy status and long-term impact on cancer. It begins the list of service delivery action points; the text is fragmented.

Lists in Chinese further action points on service delivery and comprehensive cervical cancer prevention, such as extending immunization services, consistent messaging, health worker training, screening and treatment, and monitoring indicators. The extracted text is fragmented.

Discusses in Chinese stewardship and financing for HPV vaccine introduction, including resource mobilisation, epidemiological evidence, demand forecasting and the importance of international commitments through GAVI, UNICEF and PAHO to expand supply and secure prices. The extracted text is heavily interleaved.

Lists in Chinese the financing action points, such as a national HPV vaccine working group, demand and cost modelling, and aligning resource mobilisation with multi-year immunization and sector-wide plans; the text is fragmented.
A short Chinese fragment on reproductive health programmes contributing to GAVI applications and WHO/UNFPA technical help for countries not eligible for GAVI.

The Chinese conclusion, stating that HPV vaccines meet an important public health need within comprehensive cervical cancer control, that equity for poorer women must be addressed, and that introduction decisions rest with countries; it also notes the 2006 FDA approval of the quadrivalent vaccine.
A Chinese list of additional resources with web links for UNFPA, WHO, GIVS and GAVI.
